mainTopic: Sales versus loans in the laws of ריבית: fixing the market price, early advance purchases and מי שפרע, payment for waiting, and extra coins found in a loan
overview: רבא concludes that produce and its money value are treated the same. So a buyer may pay now at today's market price even if the seller has no produce yet. He answers a challenge from a ברייתא by saying it deals with paying back a loan, while his case is a plain sale. רבה and רב יוסף explain that the buyer gains nothing special, since with cash he could buy cheaply nearby. When אביי asks why the same logic would not permit lending a סאה for a סאה, רב יוסף answers that a loan is different from a sale. אדא בר אבא objects that the buyer saves a broker's fee. רבא says the buyer pays that fee too, and רב אשי says cash does the broker's job anyway. Next, someone who pays at the early advance price must show himself to the seller so the seller relies on the deal and the curse of מי שפרע applies. רב אשי adds that meeting him in the market is enough. Finally, רב נחמן teaches that any payment for waiting is ריבית. He rules on a discount from a wax seller, which is allowed only if the seller already has the wax and not if he only has credit in town. He also rules on extra coins found in a loan, and the גמרא begins to define how much extra counts as a possible mistake.

steps.title: Produce and its value are treated the same, so one may set a price by the market rate
steps.stepSummary: רבא concludes that produce and its value are interchangeable in both directions. Therefore one may fix a price by the market rate even without owning the produce.
steps.simpleTranslation: Just as we say, 'What difference does it make to me, the produce or its value,' we also say, 'What difference does it make to me, its value or the produce.' Therefore one may set a price by the market rate, even though he does not have the produce.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא finishes his teaching. Since produce and money are treated as equal, a person may lock in today's market price for produce he will deliver later, even if he has none right now.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An earlier principle said produce can be swapped for its value. רבא says the swap works both ways. So money paid now at the market rate counts as if the produce were already there. Since the produce is easy to buy on the market, it is as though the seller already has it.

keyTerms.term: מָה לִי הֵן וּמָה לִי דְּמֵיהֶן
keyTerms.meaning: What difference does it make: the items themselves or their value
One may set or fix a price

phrases.aramaic: מָה לִי הֵן וּמָה לִי דְּמֵיהֶן – אָמְרִינַן,
phrases.english: [Since] we say: what difference to me, them or their value,

phrases.aramaic: מָה לִי דְּמֵיהֶן וּמָה לִי הֵן – נָמֵי אָמְרִינַן.
phrases.english: we also say: what difference to me, their value or them.
And one may set a price by the market rate,
even though he does not have [the produce].

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה לִי הֵן וּמָה לִי דְּמֵיהֶן – אָמְרִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבא's teaching, which began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Produce and its value are interchangeable both ways, so one may fix a price at the market rate even without owning the produce.

steps.title: A ברייתא says it is forbidden if he does not have the produce
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא and רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע challenge רבא from a ברייתא that forbids the deal when the person has no produce.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא and רב הונא son of רב יהושע raised an objection to רבא: In all of these cases, if he has the produce it is permitted, and if he does not have it, it is forbidden!
steps.whatsHappening: Two sages quote a ברייתא that seems to say the opposite of רבא. It says that if he has no produce, the deal is forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא just said that not having the produce does not matter. The ברייתא clearly makes having it the deciding factor. So it looks like רבא's ruling clashes with an earlier source.

keyTerms.meaning: He raised an objection to him from an earlier source
All of them (all the cases in that ברייתא)

phrases.english: Rav Pappa raised an objection

phrases.aramaic: וְרַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ לְרָבָא:
phrases.english: and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua, to Rava:
All of them: if he has [the produce], it is permitted,
if he does not have it, it is forbidden!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵיתִיבֵיהּ רַב פָּפָּא וְרַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ לְרָבָא
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling that one may fix a price even without having the produce
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא explicitly forbids the deal when he does not have the produce, which contradicts רבא.

steps.title: There it is a loan, here it is a sale
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the ברייתא is about paying back a loan, while his ruling is about a simple sale.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: There it is a loan; here it is a sale.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא explains that the two sources are talking about different kinds of deals, so they do not clash.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא there is already a loan, and the borrower is turning his debt into produce. That raises a worry about ריבית, so having the produce matters. In רבא's case there is no loan at all, just a purchase, so this worry does not apply.

phrases.english: He said to them: There it is a loan,
phrases.notes: 'There' is the ברייתא, which is about paying back a loan someone already owes.

phrases.english: here it is a sale.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ: הָתָם הַלְוָאָה, הָכָא זְבִינֵי
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to cover every kind of deal, including a plain sale.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is only about converting a loan. A plain sale at the market rate is allowed even without the produce.
steps.whatToRemember: A loan raises ריבית worries, but a straightforward sale does not. That is why the rules differ.

steps.title: Why fixing the market price is allowed: the buyer gains nothing special
steps.stepSummary: רבה and רב יוסף explain that the buyer gets no real benefit from the deal, because with cash he could buy cheaply in nearby markets anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה and רב יוסף both say: What is the reason the חכמים said one may set a price by the market rate even though he does not have the produce? Because he says to him: 'Your favor is taken and thrown on the thorns. How have you helped me? If I had money in my hands, I would buy cheaply in הִינֵי and שִׁילֵי.'
steps.whatsHappening: Two sages give the reason behind the rule. Locking in the market price is not a hidden reward for the buyer's money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry is that the buyer pays early and gets a benefit in return, which would look like ריבית. But the buyer can honestly say the 'favor' is worthless to him, since cheap produce is easy to get in the nearby markets. Since there is no real gain, there is no ריבית.

keyTerms.meaning: Your favor is taken (I get nothing from it)

phrases.english: Rabba and Rav Yosef both say:
What is the reason the Sages said
one may set a price by the market rate
even though he does not have it?
Because he says to him: Your favor is taken
phrases.notes: The buyer is talking to the seller here.

phrases.english: and thrown on the thorns.
phrases.notes: It's a saying: your 'favor' is worthless to me.

phrases.english: How have you helped me?
If I had money in my hands,
I would buy in Hini and Shili cheaply.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּה וְרַב יוֹסֵף דְּאָמְרִי תַּרְוַיְיהוּ: מַאי טַעְמָא אֲמַרוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the underlying reason for the rule in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Fixing the market price is allowed because the buyer gets no real benefit, since cheap produce is available elsewhere.

steps.title: Then lending a סאה for a סאה should also be allowed
steps.stepSummary: אביי challenges רב יוסף: by the same logic, lending produce to be paid back with the same amount of produce should be permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to רב יוסף: If so, it should be permitted to lend a סאה for a סאה, since the lender can say: 'Your favor is taken and thrown on the thorns,' because he says to him: 'Would my wheat have burned up in my storehouse?'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי takes רב יוסף's reasoning and applies it to a case everyone knows is forbidden, lending סאה בסאה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Lending a סאה to get back a סאה is forbidden, because the price might go up, and then the lender would gain. אביי argues that the lender could also say he gains nothing, since his wheat would have kept its value in storage anyway. So if 'no real gain' permits the sale, it should permit this loan too.

keyTerms.meaning: But if that is so (then something strange follows)
A סאה of produce to be repaid with a סאה

phrases.english: Abaye said to Rav Yosef:

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה מוּתָּר לִלְוֹת סְאָה בִּסְאָה,
phrases.english: But if so, it should be permitted to lend a se'a for a se'a,
since he can say to him:
phrases.notes: Now it is the lender talking to the borrower.

phrases.english: Your favor is taken and thrown on the thorns,
for he says to him: Is it wheat that would burn up in my storehouse?
phrases.notes: He means my wheat would have stayed safe in storage, so I gained nothing by lending it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי לְרַב יוֹסֵף: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reasoning given in step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's reasoning that 'your favor is worthless' permits the deal
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same reasoning would permit סאה בסאה, which is known to be forbidden.

steps.title: A loan is different from a sale
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף answers that סאה בסאה is a loan, which is stricter, while his case is a sale.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: There it is a loan; here it is a sale.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף uses the same answer רבא gave earlier: the 'no real gain' reasoning works for a sale, not for a loan.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a loan, any possible gain to the lender is a ריבית problem, so the excuse that the favor is worthless does not help. With a sale, there is no lender and borrower, so that reasoning is enough to permit it.

phrases.english: He said to him: There it is a loan,
here it is a sale.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָתָם הַלְוָאָה, הָכָא – זְבִינֵי
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The reasoning that the favor is worthless should apply equally to loans.
steps.terutzMaskana: That reasoning only permits a sale. A loan like סאה בסאה stays forbidden.
steps.whatToRemember: The same dividing line appears twice: a loan is strict about ריבית, while a sale at the market rate is allowed even without the produce.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two speakers who give this answer. In step 3 it is רבא, and here it is רב יוסף, but the distinction is the same.

steps.title: Doesn't the buyer save a broker's fee?
steps.stepSummary: אדא בר אבא challenges רבא: the buyer does gain from paying early, because otherwise he would have to pay a broker.
steps.simpleTranslation: אדא בר אבא said to רבא: But he would need to pay money to a broker!
steps.whatsHappening: אדא בר אבא raises a new objection. He says the buyer really does gain something from paying early.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier we said the buyer gains nothing, because he could just buy cheaply with his cash in nearby markets. אדא בר אבא points out that buying elsewhere costs a broker's fee. So paying early saves him that fee, and that looks like a hidden benefit, which is a problem of ריבית.

keyTerms.meaning: a broker or middleman who arranges purchases for a fee
but he needs to... (opening of a challenge)

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַדָּא בַּר אַבָּא לְרָבָא:
phrases.english: Adda bar Abba said to Rava:
But he would need to give money to a broker!
phrases.notes: He means the buyer: if he went to buy elsewhere he'd pay a broker, so the early deal saves him that cost.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the claim from step 4 that the buyer gains no real benefit.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling (step 1) that one may fix a price at the market rate, and the claim from step 4 behind it that the buyer gets no benefit because he could buy cheaply elsewhere with cash.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Buying elsewhere costs a broker's fee, so the early deal does save the buyer money, which is a benefit.

steps.title: The buyer pays the broker's fee too
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the case is where the buyer also pays the seller an amount equal to the broker's fee.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: It is a case where he also gives him that.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the objection. He limits his ruling to a case where the buyer pays the seller the broker's fee as well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the buyer pays the seller what a broker would have cost, he saves nothing. That removes the hidden benefit, so the deal is still permitted.

phrases.english: He said to him:
Where he gives him that too.
phrases.notes: The buyer also gives the seller the amount of the broker's fee, so he gains nothing.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: The buyer saves the broker's fee and so benefits.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ruling applies where the buyer also pays the seller the broker's fee, so there is no saving.

steps.title: Cash works as its own broker
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי gives a different answer: someone with cash in hand doesn't need a broker at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: A person's money itself acts as his broker.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a second answer to the broker objection. He says there is no broker's fee to save in the first place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא needed the buyer to pay the fee. רב אשי says that is not necessary, because sellers come to someone holding cash. Since the buyer would never pay a broker anyway, the early deal saves him nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: his brokering, the job of a broker

steps.whatToRemember: Two answers to the broker objection: רבא says the buyer pays the fee too, and רב אשי says cash in hand makes a broker unnecessary.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
People's money
itself does the broker's job for him.
phrases.notes: The ready cash does it: someone holding cash finds sellers easily, so he never needs a broker.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: זוּזֵי דְּאִינָשֵׁי אִינְהוּ עָבְדִי לֵיהּ סַפְסֵירוּתֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different answer to step 7's challenge than רבא's in step 8.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The buyer would need a broker, so he saves a fee.
steps.terutzMaskana: Cash makes a broker unnecessary, so there is no saving even without extra payment.

steps.title: Early buyer must show himself at the threshing floor
steps.stepSummary: רבה and רב יוסף rule that someone who pays early at the advance price must show himself at the seller's threshing floor.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה and רב יוסף both say: One who gives money at the advance price must show himself at the threshing floor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new, related teaching about someone who pays early for produce at the advance price. It says he has to show up at the threshing floor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This opens a new topic: what the buyer must do after paying early. The ruling is stated without a reason, and the next step will ask for one.

keyTerms.meaning: the early advance price, set before the regular market price
to show oneself, to be seen

phrases.english: Rabbah and Rav Yosef, who both say:
One who gives money
at the advance price,
phrases.notes: Literally, "the sharp gate." It means the early price right after harvest, before the market price is set.

phrases.english: must show himself at the threshing floor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new, related teaching about early purchases of produce.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A buyer who pays at the advance price must appear at the seller's threshing floor.

steps.title: Why does he need to show up?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why showing up matters. It doesn't complete the purchase, and the curse of מי שפרע applies even without it.
steps.simpleTranslation: For what purpose? If it is to acquire, he doesn't acquire that way. If it is to make the seller subject to "מי שפרע," the seller is subject to "מי שפרע" even when the buyer doesn't show up!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the ruling. It tries two possible reasons and knocks both down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: First option: showing up completes the purchase. It doesn't, because being there is not a valid קנין. Second option: it makes the seller subject to the curse of מי שפרע if he backs out. But that curse already applies once money was paid, so showing up seems pointless.

keyTerms.meaning: the curse on someone who backs out of a deal after money was paid
to have him accept upon himself

steps.confusionAlert: Paying money alone does not complete a purchase of movable goods; the buyer has to pull the item. That is why backing out is possible at all, and why the curse of מי שפרע comes up.

phrases.english: For what purpose?
If it is to acquire — he doesn't acquire that way,
phrases.notes: Just standing at the threshing floor is not a way of acquiring the produce.

phrases.english: If it is so the seller accepts "He Who exacted payment" upon himself,
phrases.notes: That's the curse on someone who backs out of a deal after taking money.

phrases.english: even when he doesn't show himself,
the seller still accepts "He Who exacted payment" upon himself!

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמַאי? אִי לְמִקְנֵא – הָא לָא קָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the purpose of the ruling in step 10.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What legal purpose the buyer's appearance at the threshing floor serves.

steps.title: Showing up tells the seller the deal is real
steps.stepSummary: It really is about מי שפרע. Early buyers often pay several sellers, so if the buyer doesn't show up, the seller can say he assumed the buyer had taken better produce elsewhere.
steps.simpleTranslation: Actually, it is about the seller accepting "מי שפרע." Someone who pays at the advance price pays two or three sellers. If he shows himself, the seller relies on the deal. If not, the seller can say: I thought you found produce nicer than mine and took it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the reason is the curse of מי שפרע after all. Showing up is what keeps that curse in force.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Early buyers commonly pay a few sellers to be safe. So a buyer who never comes gives the seller a fair excuse: "I figured you went with someone else." When the buyer appears, the seller knows the deal is live, and backing out would bring the curse of מי שפרע.

keyTerms.meaning: actually, really (keeping one of the earlier options)
his mind relies, he counts on it

steps.whatToRemember: An early buyer must show up at the threshing floor so the seller knows the deal is real. Otherwise the seller can say he thought the buyer bought elsewhere, and the curse of מי שפרע would not apply.
steps.whyThisMatters: The curse of מי שפרע applies only when the seller truly knows the buyer is counting on the deal. A real excuse to think the deal was off can protect him.

phrases.english: Actually, it is so the seller accepts "He Who exacted payment" upon himself,
and one who gives money at the advance price,
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets is part of the corrected wording, so read it as part of the line.

phrases.english: gives it to two or three places,
if he shows himself to him, the seller relies on the deal,
but if not, the seller can say to him:
I thought that you found produce
nicer than mine, and you took it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 11 by keeping the second option and explaining why showing up matters.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The appearance keeps the curse of מי שפרע in force, since without it the seller has a fair excuse to think the buyer bought elsewhere.

steps.title: Meeting the seller in the market is enough
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says that since the reason is the seller's reliance, the buyer can reassure him anywhere, even in the market.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: Now that you said the reason is that the seller relies on the buyer, then even if the buyer finds him in the market and tells him, the seller relies on him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי takes the answer from the last step and draws a practical conclusion from it. The buyer does not have to go to the threshing floor; telling the seller in the market works too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 12 said the point of showing up is so the seller knows the buyer is still counting on him, so מי שפרע can apply. If that is the whole reason, the place does not matter. Any clear message that the buyer stands behind the deal does the same job.

keyTerms.meaning: Now that you have said: a formula for drawing a conclusion from an earlier answer
Relying, having one's mind settled on the deal

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
Now that you said it is because of relying,
phrases.notes: This points back to the answer just given: the seller has to know the buyer is still counting on him.

phrases.english: even if he found him in the market and told him,
he relies on him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר רב אשי השתא דאמרת משום מסמך דעתא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a practical conclusion from the reason given in Step 12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The buyer does not need to go to the threshing floor. Telling the seller anywhere, even in the market, makes the seller rely on him.

steps.title: The general rule: paying for waiting is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן gives a basic rule of ריבית: any payment for waiting is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: The general rule of ריבית is that any payment for waiting is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: A new section begins. רב נחמן gives one short rule that covers all of ריבית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If someone gets extra money or goods only because he waited for his money, that extra is ריבית. This rule explains the cases that come next. A discount for paying early can turn into a payment for waiting.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the basic test for spotting ריבית in many situations, including sales and not only loans.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said:
The general rule of interest:
any payment for waiting for him is forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic: a general principle of ריבית.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Any payment given in exchange for waiting for money is forbidden as ריבית.

steps.title: Paying a wax seller early for a discount
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן rules that a seller may give a discount for early payment only if he already has the wax.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן also said: Someone gives money to a wax seller. The price is four pieces for a coin, and the seller says, 'I will give you five for a coin.' If the seller has the wax, it is permitted. If he does not have it, it is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן gives a real case. A buyer pays early and gets five pieces of wax instead of the usual four.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the seller already has the wax, this is a sale at a cheap price, and that is allowed. If he does not have it, the money works like a loan. The extra piece is then payment for waiting, which is the rule from Step 14.

keyTerms.meaning: He does not have them with him

phrases.english: And Rav Nachman said:
This one who gives money to a wax seller,
and they are going at four for each coin,
phrases.notes: The market price right now is four pieces of wax for each coin.

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲמַר לֵיהּ: יָהֵיבְנָא לָךְ חֲמֵשׁ חֲמֵשׁ,
phrases.english: and he said to him: I will give you five for each,
if he has them with him, it is permitted;
if he does not have them with him, it is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: ואמר רב נחמן האי מאן דיהיב זוזי לקיראה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the general rule of payment for waiting to a sale case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A discount for early payment is allowed only if the seller already has the goods. Otherwise it is ריבית.

steps.title: Isn't this obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב נחמן needed to say the wax ruling, since it seems obvious.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב נחמן's wax ruling, saying it is too obvious to need saying. This sets up the next step, which explains what the ruling teaches.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the seller has no wax, the money is plainly a loan, and the extra piece is plainly payment for waiting. So the גמרא asks what new point רב נחמן is adding.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious: a challenge asking what a statement adds

phrases.english: It is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether Step 15 needed to be said.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ruling seems to say only what we already know from the basic rule of ריבית, so it looks unnecessary.

steps.title: The case is a seller with credit in town
steps.stepSummary: The ruling is needed for a seller who has credit in town. You might think that counts as having the wax, but it does not, because he still has to collect it.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed where the seller has credit in town. You might have said: since he has credit in town, it is like 'until my son comes' or 'until I find the key.' So רב נחמן teaches us that since the wax still has to be collected, it is as if he does not have it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It explains the new point: having credit in town is not the same as having the wax.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A seller who really has the goods but cannot reach them right now, for example 'until my son comes,' counts as having them. You might think credit in town is just as good. רב נחמן teaches that it is not: the wax still has to be collected, so it counts as not there, and the discount is ריבית.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for a special case

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up 'my son is coming' or 'I can't find the key' with having credit. In the first cases the seller owns the goods already. With credit, he still has to collect them, so he does not count as having them.
steps.whatToRemember: A seller counts as 'having' the goods only if they are already his, even if they are hard to reach right now. Goods he still has to collect count as not his yet, so a discount for early payment is ריבית.

steps.title: Finding extra coins in a loan
steps.stepSummary: If a borrower finds extra coins, he must return them if the extra could be a mistake. If not, it is a gift.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן also said: Someone borrows coins from his friend and finds extra among them. If the extra is an amount a person could easily miscount, he must return it. If not, it is just a gift the lender gave him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן gives one more ruling about loans. It is about a borrower who finds more coins than he agreed to borrow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling depends on how big the extra is. A small extra is probably a counting mistake, so it must go back. A large extra could not be a mistake, so we assume the lender meant it as a gift.

keyTerms.meaning: An amount a person could easily get wrong

phrases.english: And Rav Nachman said:
This one who borrowed coins from his friend
and found extra in it:
if it is an amount a person could mistake,
he must return it to him;
and if not,
it is merely a gift that he gave him.

steps.triggerLanguage: ואמר רב נחמן האי מאן דאוזיף פשיטי מחבריה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another ruling from רב נחמן about loans.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Extra coins small enough to be a counting mistake must be returned. A larger extra is treated as a gift.

steps.title: How much extra counts as a possible mistake?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the exact case of 'within the range of a mistake' from step 18, and introduces רב אחא בריה דרב יוסף, who will answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: What exactly is a case of 'an amount someone could mistakenly give'? רב אחא, the son of רב יוסף, said:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a clear, concrete example of the phrase 'בכדי שהדעת טועה' from the last ruling. This step sets up the next move: רב אחא בריה דרב יוסף is about to give the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 18 said the borrower must return the extra only if it could be an honest mistake, but did not say how much extra that is. The גמרא now asks for a real-life measure, so we know when the money must go back and when it is a gift. Only the name of the one answering appears here; his actual answer comes next.
